cs.t:
1st Word on the Atari ST 520+ with monochrome monitor: that
was how the far future felt like in 1986. With the exception of the somewhat wobbly cheap keyboard, that was the best and most distraction-free setup I have ever seen for WYSIWYG word processing (sadly never tried the Xerox workstations).
cs.th: In memory of the man who put red and green squiggles under words

but I recall having a very fond time on the Atari ST 520+.
It had one of the best b/w monitors and TOS+GEM was orderly and uncluttered. Only preemptive multitasking and per-window menus were missing. As a plus, the OS was in ROM, so boot times were <1s.
> who's keyboard was frankly Not Very Good I dunno man. I came from a ZX Spectrum (via several other machines, it's true) and compared to that, the ST keyboard was  great .

I owned one of those!  I sold my 1040ST to my friend to get some of the money for a Mega 2. I liked how the keyboard was detachable and the hard drive was the same size at the motherboard case, so you could stack them.

Ah memories... and my personal progress over time: My very first calculator: [0] My first slide rule: [1] (for two years or so, then we switched to electronic calculators) Before I could afford a computer I spent a a few years on computers I didn't own, ZX Spectrum, C64, C128, 8bit Atari, KC85/1,2,3, but also LC 80 [2] My 1st (own) computer: East German 8 bit KC85/4 with the CAOS operating system (the makers had a good sense of humor, it means "Cassette-Aided OS") [3][4]. Mass-storage was ones regular stereo cassette radio recorder, a floppy disc drive was available but rare. My 2nd computer: Atari 1040 STFM [5] - bought with my first West German money after reunification! Finally 16 bit! Atari ST software worth mentioning: "Script 2" was a wonderful word processor for Atari [6]. When used in combination with the (for the time) excellent black/white monitor and a 24 needle printer (Epson LQ 580) I got near laser printer quality through the special drivers of that program. Worst Atari incident: I had a capacitor (literally) blow up on me with a very loud  BANG! . I'll end with the Atari. The next one - for my studies - was a 486DX33 8MB RAM machine with Windows 3.1, soon RedHat Linux (1995). Thanks to the student network I could start large programs like Netscape on another student's Pentium PC (in another building) and export the display until I was able to upgrade to 16 MB RAM... and all the usual mid-1990s Unix systems, also available remotely thanks to the network. cs.t: The main problem with the keyboard was the non-standard size of the kepcaps. The standard distance between keycaps is 0.75 inches, and the standard top width is 0.5 inches. The Atari ST keycap distance is standard, but the top width is 0.625 inches. Because of this, if your finger isn't exactly centered over the top of the key, it hits the adjacent key too, leading to key jam.
cs.th: Atari Means Business with the Mega ST
